name: Cold water rinse

chain: Cold water at end of wash
angle.text: Proponents finish washes with cold water in the belief that it closes the cuticle and adds shine. The idea is popular in hair-care circles; nobody has published a test of the shine effect.

summary: Finishing the wash with cold water, said to add shine by closing the cuticle; nobody has published a test of it.
note: Cuticle-closing claim has no published study behind it.
currentQuick:
A cold water rinse means finishing a hair wash with cool or cold water. People who do it say it leaves hair shinier and smoother.
The idea rests on the belief that cold water closes the cuticle. No studies of the practice on hair were found.
How it works: The practice is a final rinse at lower temperature. The proposed explanation is that the outer cuticle scales lie flatter, reflecting more light.
Risks and caveats: No documented harms specific to the practice were found. Cold exposure itself may be uncomfortable for some people.
deepLead:
A cold water rinse is a hair-care habit of finishing a wash with cool or cold water. Proponents say it makes hair look shinier and smoother, with the reasoning that cold water closes or flattens the hair cuticle.
Wikipedia's article on hair care describes the cuticle as part of a shaft with no living processes, so care focuses on keeping it intact, and notes that chemical processing can leave the cuticle unable to close fully . The article does not discuss water temperature, and no published studies of cold water rinses on hair shine or smoothness were found.

name: Apple cider vinegar rinse

angle.text: Users pour diluted apple cider vinegar over hair after washing, promoted as clarifying buildup and adding shine. The appearance claim rests on anecdote and has not been tested in trials.

summary: A diluted vinegar rinse after shampooing, said to clarify and add shine; supported only by anecdote, with burn and irritation reports for strong vinegar.
note: Undiluted vinegar has caused chemical burns; eye contact is a documented hazard.
currentQuick:
An ACV rinse is diluted apple cider vinegar poured over hair after washing. People who use it say it removes buildup and makes hair shinier and smoother.
A 2025 review in Cutis called the method an anecdotal remedy lacking supporting data, and no trials on natural hair were found.
How it works: The theory is that the acetic acid, about 5 percent of the vinegar, lowers the pH of the hair surface, which proponents say flattens the cuticle and dissolves residue. Studies of vinegar rinses specifically have not been published.
Risks and caveats: Vinegar is acidic. Wikipedia lists eye irritation, possible corneal injury and skin burns with topical use, and product labels advise dilution. Allergy is possible in people allergic to apples.
deepLead:
An apple cider vinegar (ACV) rinse is a home hair treatment in which diluted apple cider vinegar is poured over the hair and scalp after washing. It is promoted as a clarifying rinse that removes product buildup, adds shine and smooths the cuticle.
Apple cider vinegar is roughly 94 percent water and 5 percent acetic acid, according to Wikipedia, which describes clinical evidence for its health uses as poor and notes that regulators and major health organizations do not recommend it for any therapeutic use . A 2025 literature review in the journal Cutis described the ACV rinse method, in the context of synthetic hair extensions, as an anecdotal remedy lacking data to support it . No controlled trials of ACV rinses on natural hair were found.

name: Rice water rinse

angle.text: Users apply fermented rice water after shampooing, with claims that it strengthens hair, reduces breakage, adds shine and helps hair grow longer. It has a long traditional use; research is thin.

summary: A starchy, often fermented rice soak used as a hair rinse; long tradition, thin research, and buildup reported on some hair types.
note: Growth claims are anecdotal; protein or starch buildup can leave hair stiff or brittle.
currentQuick:
Rice water rinse means pouring the liquid from soaked, rinsed or boiled rice, often fermented, over hair after shampoo. It has a long traditional reputation in parts of Asia and is popular today for claimed strength, shine and length.
AI-generated Grokipedia reports no strong evidence that it lengthens hair, and says the small trials that exist mostly studied rice bran products.
How it works: Believers credit inositol, amino acids and starch, which are said to coat or enter the shaft, reducing friction and breakage. Fermentation adds acidity. The mechanisms are proposed rather than confirmed for rice water.
Risks and caveats: Reported downsides include protein or starch buildup causing dryness, stiffness and brittleness, especially in curly hair. Rice can carry arsenic, a concern mainly for ingestion. Spoiled rice water is described as something to discard.
deepLead:
A rice water rinse is a hair treatment in which the starchy liquid left from soaking, rinsing or boiling rice, often fermented for a day or two, is applied to the hair and scalp after shampooing. Proponents say it strengthens hair, reduces breakage and adds shine, and some say it helps hair grow longer .
Wikipedia states that women in China, Japan and Southeast Asia have reportedly used rice water on hair for centuries, and that women in Japan's Heian period (794-1185) were reportedly able to grow very long hair by soaking it in rice water . Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, says there is no strong scientific evidence that fermented rice water lengthens hair or speeds growth, that claims are largely anecdotal (including those associated with Yao women in Huangluo, China), and that studies of rice water itself are limited or low quality .

name: Egg hair mask

angle.text: An egg mask is used at home as a kitchen-ingredient protein treatment for dry, damaged or weak-feeling hair. It is popular in hair-care circles, and no trials have tested it.

summary: A kitchen protein mask for hair; popular at home, with no trials behind it.
note: Raw egg carries Salmonella and allergy concerns.
currentQuick:
An egg hair mask means applying raw egg, or its white or yolk, to the hair for a while and then rinsing it out. It is promoted as a home protein treatment for dry or damaged hair.
No clinical studies of egg masks on hair were found. General reviews of conditioners say protein effects on hair are temporary.
How it works: Proponents attribute the effect to the protein in egg. Conditioner science describes protein treatments as coating or filling the hair surface, with effects that wash out.
Risks and caveats: Eggs are a common allergen and raw eggs can carry Salmonella, according to food-safety guidance. Evidence for hair benefit is limited to general conditioner knowledge.
deepLead:
An egg hair mask is a home hair-care treatment in which raw egg, or its white or yolk, is applied to the hair and scalp for a period before being rinsed out. It is promoted as a protein treatment for dry, damaged or weak-feeling hair, and is discussed in hair-care circles as a kitchen-ingredient alternative to commercial protein conditioners.
Eggs are chiefly water and protein in the white and fat in the yolk . Commercial conditioners that use protein typically rely on hydrolysed protein fragments, and an encyclopedia overview of conditioners states that such protein effects are temporary because shampooing removes excess protein . No clinical trial of egg masks on hair was identified, and the evidence for this specific practice is limited to general knowledge about conditioning and food safety.
Health agencies advise that raw eggs can carry Salmonella and that eggs are a common food allergen .

name: Castor oil

chain: Thick oil on hair, brows, lashes
angle.text: Users rub castor oil on scalp, brows and lashes in hopes of thicker, longer growth, and the oil also coats hair like a conditioner. It is established as a laxative; its growth effect on hair is untested.

summary: A thick pressed seed oil people rub on hair, brows and lashes; established as a laxative, untested for growth.
note: Oral use causes cramping and diarrhoea; no hair-growth trials found.
currentQuick:
Castor oil is a viscous oil pressed from castor beans. It is sold as an over-the-counter laxative and used in cosmetics and industry.
Looksmaxxers apply it to scalp, brows and lashes hoping for thicker growth. Users report mixed results, and no clinical trials on hair growth were found.
How it works: Proponents say it moisturises and thickens strands. Its main component, ricinoleic acid, makes it very viscous. A hair-growth mechanism has not been shown in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Taken orally it commonly causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, and labels advise against use with abdominal pain. A pregnancy reference advises against use in pre-term pregnancy. Ricin from the raw bean is not in the processed oil.
deepLead:
Castor oil is a thick, pale vegetable oil pressed from the seeds of the castor plant, Ricinus communis. About 90 percent of its fatty acids are ricinoleates . It has been used for centuries as a laxative and today also serves as an industrial raw material and cosmetic ingredient .
In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed mainly as a topical oil applied to hair, eyebrows and eyelashes, where proponents say it thickens growth. The Wikipedia article on castor oil makes no hair claims, and no clinical trial of castor oil for hair growth appears in the sources reviewed .
Its established medical use is oral, as a stimulant laxative; the US label for an over-the-counter product lists temporary relief of occasional constipation .

name: Ayurvedic amla / bhringraj / shikakai

chain: Traditional herbs as oils or pastes
angle.text: Amla, bhringraj and shikakai are Ayurvedic herbs used as powders, pastes or oils for cleansing and conditioning hair, and promoted for hair strength and growth. They have centuries of traditional use and no clinical hair trials.

summary: Traditional Ayurvedic hair herbs; centuries of use, no clinical hair trials.
note: Traditional use; no high-quality clinical research on hair.
currentQuick:
Amla, bhringraj and shikakai are plants from the Ayurvedic tradition used as hair powders, pastes and oils. Amla is a vitamin C-rich fruit, bhringraj is Eclipta prostrata, and shikakai is a pod used as a mild cleanser.
Traditional users say they cleanse, condition and promote growth. Laboratory work exists on amla antioxidants, but no clinical hair trials were found.
How it works: Amla's tannins and vitamin C are the basis for antioxidant claims in laboratory studies. Shikakai-type plants are said to cleanse through natural saponins. Hair-growth mechanisms have not been shown in people.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed give no safety data for topical hair use. Wikipedia says no high-quality clinical research supports traditional uses of bhringraj.
deepLead:
Amla, bhringraj and shikakai are three plant materials from the Ayurvedic tradition of South Asia that are used in hair care, commonly as powders, pastes or infused oils. Amla is the fruit of Phyllanthus emblica (Indian gooseberry); bhringraj usually refers to Eclipta prostrata; shikakai is a pod-bearing plant used as a mild natural cleanser.
Practitioners of traditional hair care say these ingredients cleanse, condition and strengthen hair and promote growth or darkening. Wikipedia notes that Eclipta prostrata has been steeped in coconut oil as a hair oil that was popular until the 1970s and that its leaves yield a black hair dye , and that there is no high-quality clinical research supporting its traditional uses .
Laboratory work on amla has examined antioxidant properties of its extract . No clinical trial of these herbs for hair growth was identified in the sources reviewed.

name: Satin bonnet / durag

angle.text: Durags and satin bonnets are worn to hold waves in place and protect hair overnight, so styles look neater the next day. They are a cultural staple of Black hair care; no clinical trials exist.

summary: The silky head wrap that holds waves and protects hair overnight; a cultural staple with no clinical trials.
note: Overly tight tying may strain edges (per Grokipedia).
currentQuick:
A durag or satin bonnet is a smooth cloth cap worn to protect hair, keep moisture in and hold wave patterns in place, especially overnight. It originated in African American grooming culture.
It is central to wave-brushing routines. No clinical studies were found on its hair-health effects.
How it works: The smooth fabric reduces friction against bedding and the snug fit compresses hair so it lies flat. Sources describe this as holding the style rather than changing hair growth.
Risks and caveats: Grokipedia says overly tight tying may cause edge breakage. Durags have also drawn dress-code bans in sports and schools.
deepLead:
A durag (also do-rag) is a close-fitting cloth head covering tied around the head to protect hair; a wave cap serves a similar purpose. Both originated in the African American community and are typically made of silk, satin, polyester or cotton . A satin bonnet is a related soft, smooth-lined cap, used for the same protective purpose.
People wear them to encourage waves, curls or locs to develop, to retain moisture, to reduce breakage and to keep patterns and braids in place during sleep . In looksmaxxing and wave-brushing circles the durag is treated as a standard part of a 360 waves routine .
The durag also has a notable cultural history, including dress-code bans in sport and schools . Evidence about its hair-health effects consists of general descriptions rather than clinical trials.

name: 360 waves / wave brush

angle.text: Wave brushing, with a durag and pomade, trains short coily hair into a ripple pattern around the whole head. The pattern builds up over weeks of consistent brushing; it is a cultural staple with no clinical research.

summary: Brush-and-durag training that coaxes coily hair into ripple patterns; cultural staple, no clinical research.
note: Aggressive brushing or tight durags may contribute to traction alopecia (per Grokipedia).
currentQuick:
360 waves are a ripple pattern brushed into short coily hair so it circles the whole head. It is trained with a soft brush, pomade or moisturiser, and a durag.
It grew out of African American barbershop and grooming culture. No clinical studies were found.
How it works: People brush the hair in circles, keep it moisturised, and compress it with a durag overnight to make it lie flat. Full patterns reportedly take months, and straighter hair often fails to form them.
Risks and caveats: Aggressive brushing or tight durag use may contribute to traction alopecia, which is generally reversible according to Grokipedia. Claims of balding from waves are described there as unsubstantiated.
deepLead:
Waves are a hairstyle for short, kinky or curly hair in which the curls are brushed or combed flat into a ripple-like pattern . '360 waves' refers to a pattern that encircles the whole head, and variants include 180, 540 and spin waves . The pattern is trained with a soft brush, moisturiser or pomade, and a durag or wave cap .
The style is associated with African American men's hair care and barbershop culture . It is discussed online by communities including r/360Waves, YouTube and TikTok .
No clinical studies on wave brushing were found. Grokipedia says direct studies of wave-specific routines are limited and that claims waves cause balding are unsubstantiated, while aggressive brushing or tight durag use may contribute to traction alopecia .

name: Hair texture powder / sea salt spray

angle.text: Sea salt spray and texture powder are used to add volume, grip and a matte, tousled finish. The change is visible immediately after styling; some users also claim the spray makes hair wavier.

summary: Salt mist and dry powder for matte, voluminous hair; cosmetic styling with no clinical research.
note: Styling products can dry hair or build up (per Wikipedia).
currentQuick:
Sea salt spray and texture powder are styling products meant to give hair volume, grip and a matte look. Sea salt spray is applied wet and powder is dusted dry.
Users share DIY sea salt sprays online. No clinical studies were found.
How it works: Styling products generally coat or swell the hair strand to create temporary body. The sources reviewed do not describe the specific formulations.
Risks and caveats: Styling products can dry hair or build up and cause dullness or breakage, according to Wikipedia. No specific safety studies on these two product types were found.
deepLead:
Texture powders and sea salt sprays are hair styling products used to add volume, grip and a matte, tousled look. Sea salt spray is a salt-and-water mist applied to damp hair, while texture powder is a fine dry powder dusted at the roots.
Wikipedia's overview of styling products lists volumisers, which add temporary volume to thin or flat hair through humectants and coating polymers . It does not specifically cover sea salt spray or texture powders . No clinical studies of either product were found.
On looksmax.org users share homemade sea salt sprays and discuss them for adding waviness .

name: Blow-dry and volumizing routine

angle.text: Looksmaxxing and grooming circles use blow-drying as a low-cost way to give hair more height and body, changing how full it looks. The lift is visible straight away and washes out.

summary: Drying hair upward with a dryer for temporary root lift; no trials, and the effect washes out.
note: Repeated high heat is described as drying hair.
currentQuick:
A blow-dry and volumizing routine means drying hair with a dryer while lifting it at the roots so the style sets with more height. It is a styling technique rather than a treatment.
No published studies were found that test it for volume. The effect is temporary.
How it works: Dryers are described as setting hair by forming temporary hydrogen bonds in each strand, which humidity and washing reverse. Nozzles and diffusers change how air and heat reach the hair.
Risks and caveats: Hair-care references note that heat from dryers can leave hair dry and brittle with heavy use. Tool-related skin reactions, such as nickel contact allergy from a brush, have been reported in case literature.
deepLead:
A blow-dry and volumizing routine is a hair-styling practice in which hair is dried with a handheld dryer, often while being lifted or directed upward at the roots, to give the hairstyle more height and body. It is discussed in looksmaxxing and grooming circles as a low-cost way to change the apparent fullness of the hair.
Hair dryers work by passing air from a fan over an electric heating element. Styling with them is described as forming temporary hydrogen bonds in each hair strand, which weaken with humidity and are undone by washing. Dryers commonly include a concentrator nozzle, a diffuser and a cool-air setting that is described as helping to set a style.
No published clinical studies were found that test blow-drying routines for volume. General hair-care references note that heat from dryers and hot irons can leave hair dry and brittle when overused.

name: Heat protectant

angle.text: Heat protectants are used before blow dryers and irons to limit damage so hair keeps its shine and smoothness. They are marketed on this basis and untested in trials.

summary: A pre-styling spray or serum sold to cushion hair from hot tools; untested in trials.
note: Product descriptions say it reduces, not eliminates, heat damage.
currentQuick:
Heat protectants are sprays, serums and leave-ins applied before blow-drying or flat-ironing. They are marketed to reduce dryness, breakage and frizz from heat.
No clinical studies were found; claims rest on product and stylist descriptions.
How it works: They are described as forming a film of silicones or polymers that slows heat reaching the hair, with water and conditioning agents spreading the heat and smoothing the cuticle.
Risks and caveats: No specific harms were identified in the reviewed material. Descriptions state the products reduce but do not eliminate damage, particularly at high temperatures.
deepLead:
Heat protectants are hair-styling products, sold as sprays, serums and leave-in treatments, that are marketed to reduce thermal damage from blow dryers, flat irons and curling irons. Descriptions say they coat the hair shaft with a film that slows heat transfer and limits moisture loss.
Many products list protection up to about 450 degrees F (232 degrees C), and some also advertise conditioning or bond-repair ingredients. Industry descriptions state that these products lessen but do not eliminate damage.
No published clinical studies were found for heat protectants in the sources reviewed, so most statements about how well they work come from product descriptions and stylist recommendations.

name: Diffuser curl drying

angle.text: Diffusers are used to dry curly, permed or fine hair with less frizz and more definition and volume. The look is visible after drying and temporary; no trials exist.

summary: A dryer attachment that spreads airflow to dry curls with less frizz; no trials, and the effect is temporary.
note: Heat can dry hair with frequent use.
currentQuick:
Diffuser curl drying uses a wide, softer airflow attachment to dry curly or wavy hair so curls keep their shape. Users say it reduces frizz and adds volume.
No clinical studies were found testing it.
How it works: The diffuser spreads the dryer's air so hair dries more slowly, at a lower temperature and with less disturbance, according to dryer references.
Risks and caveats: Heat from dryers can leave hair dry and brittle with heavy use, according to hair-care references.
deepLead:
Diffuser curl drying is the practice of drying hair with a hair-dryer attachment that spreads the airflow, usually to keep curls and waves defined while adding volume. It is discussed as a styling method for naturally curly, permed and fine hair.
A diffuser is described in dryer references as spreading the airflow so that hair dries more slowly, at a lower temperature and with less disturbance, which is said to reduce frizz and add volume.
No published clinical studies were found on diffusing for curl definition.

name: Shower filter

angle.text: Shower filters are bought to reduce chlorine, which retailers link to dry skin and brittle hair. The skin and hair benefits are anecdotal.

summary: A chlorine-reducing filter for the shower arm; the skin and hair benefits are anecdotal.
note: A hospital study found bacterial contamination of one filter type.
currentQuick:
Shower filters attach to the shower arm to reduce chlorine in the water. People use them hoping for softer skin and hair.
No trials on skin or hair appearance were found, and descriptions call the evidence limited and anecdotal.
How it works: Water passes through media such as KDF, calcium sulfite and activated carbon that react with or adsorb chlorine before it exits the showerhead.
Risks and caveats: A 2022 hospital study reported that hollow-fibre shower filters did not prevent patient exposure to Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Cartridges are described as needing periodic replacement.
deepLead:
A shower filter is a point-of-use water filter fitted at the shower arm, either as an inline unit or as a showerhead with built-in media, intended to reduce contaminants in shower water, chiefly chlorine. Retail marketing frames them as a way to ease dry skin and brittle hair attributed to chlorinated or hard water.
Descriptions say certified models are tested under the NSF/ANSI 177 standard for free available chlorine, and typically use media such as KDF, calcium sulfite and activated carbon. The same description states that scientific evidence for skin and hair benefits is limited and largely anecdotal.
No clinical trials of shower filters for skin or hair appearance were found. Hospital research has examined shower filters for a different purpose, bacterial exposure.

name: Scalp exfoliation

angle.text: Users exfoliate the scalp to clear flakes and product buildup, and some say it supports hair growth. There is some flaking data; no hair-growth trials exist.

summary: Scrubs and acids to clear scalp flakes and buildup; some flaking data, no hair-growth trials.
currentQuick:
Scalp exfoliation uses scrubs or acids to remove dead skin and buildup. People use it for flaking and hoping for healthier hair.
Salicylic acid is an approved dandruff active, but no trials tested exfoliation for hair growth.
How it works: Physical granules rub debris off; acids such as salicylic or glycolic acid loosen bonds between dead skin cells.
Risks and caveats: Descriptions say overdoing it may cause dryness, oiliness or irritation, and that people with psoriasis, eczema or open sores should consult a dermatologist.
deepLead:
Scalp exfoliation is a hair-care practice that uses physical scrubs, chemical exfoliants such as salicylic or glycolic acid, or hybrids to remove dead skin cells, oil and product buildup from the scalp. Proponents say it reduces flaking, helps products absorb and supports hair growth.
Salicylic acid is an FDA-approved over-the-counter anti-dandruff active, and dandruff shampoos combine actives such as zinc pyrithione and ketoconazole. Physical scalp scrubs are not covered in that reference.
One 2024 study evaluated a hydroxy acid scrub combined with a copper tripeptide serum in adults with seborrheic dermatitis. No studies were found testing scalp exfoliation for hair growth.

name: Protein intake for hair

angle.text: Hair and looksmaxxing communities suggest eating enough protein to support hair growth and quality, since hair is largely keratin. Deficiency links are noted; no trials test extra protein for hair.

summary: Eating enough protein for hair; deficiency links are noted, but no trials test extra protein.
note: References link deficiency, not extra intake, to hair changes.
currentQuick:
The idea is that because hair is keratin, adequate dietary protein supports hair. References note deficiencies can show up in hair.
No studies were found testing extra protein for hair in people with normal intake.
How it works: Hair is made of keratin protein, so growth is thought to depend on adequate nutrition.
Risks and caveats: References do not report specific harms; hair-loss references note evidence for supplements is insufficient, and deficiencies like iron or B12 are cited as causes of hair loss.
deepLead:
Protein intake for hair is the idea that eating enough protein supports hair growth and quality, because hair is made largely of keratin. It is discussed in lifestyle sections of hair and looksmaxxing communities.
General hair-care references state that a balanced diet matters and that deficiencies often show first in hair, naming protein, iron, zinc, biotin and other nutrients as linked to dryness, shedding or weak hair, though much of that text is uncited. The same reference says shampoos or vitamins have not been shown to noticeably change growth rate.
Dermatology references list malnutrition, vitamin B12 deficiency and iron deficiency among causes of non-scarring hair loss, and state that supplements are not typically recommended for hair loss and that there is no evidence for biotin.

name: Gelatin / bone broth

chain: Building blocks for skin and hair
angle.text: Fans eat gelatin and bone broth in the belief that collagen supports skin and hair. The published record on appearance benefits is essentially empty.

summary: Collagen-rich foods that fans tie to skin and hair; the published record on appearance benefits is essentially empty.
note: Reference sources report no established benefit for ingested collagen on joints; no studies of appearance effects were found.
currentQuick:
Gelatin and bone broth are foods made from animal collagen. Some wellness and appearance communities treat them as a way to support skin, hair and joints.
Reference sources report no established cause-and-effect link for joints, and no studies of appearance outcomes were found for this entry.
How it works: Simmering animal bones and connective tissue turns collagen into gelatin. Proponents reason that eating collagen-derived amino acids supplies building blocks for skin and hair; this mechanism has not been tested in published appearance trials.
Risks and caveats: Gelatin is a protein food and is generally treated as low risk, though some people are allergic to gelatin in injected drugs and it is not suitable for vegetarian, halal or kosher practice depending on source [2].
deepLead:
Gelatin and bone broth are collagen-derived foods. Gelatin is made by partially breaking down animal collagen, mostly from pork skin, bones and cattle hides, and gels in water . Bone broth is a long-simmered stock of animal bones and connective tissue, in which collagen converts to gelatin and thickens the liquid .
In looksmaxxing and wellness circles they are discussed as dietary "collagen foods" that proponents associate with skin, hair and joint appearance. Regulators and reference sources report that a cause-and-effect link between ingested collagen hydrolysate and joint maintenance has not been established, and one encyclopedia summary states there is no scientific evidence supporting many of the health claims made for bone broth .

name: Brushing technique (boar bristle)

angle.text: Boar bristle brushes are used to smooth hair and are said to spread scalp oil along the strands for shine. The smoothing is a styling effect; the oil-distribution claim has no published tests.

summary: Natural-bristle brushing for smoothness and shine; the oil-distribution claim has no published tests behind it.
note: No studies of oil distribution or shine were found.
currentQuick:
A boar bristle brush uses natural bristles that are tightly spaced to smooth hair. Fans say it spreads scalp oil and adds shine.
Reference sources describe the smoothing design but do not report oil-distribution effects.
How it works: Tight bristles create tension that smooths strands. Proponents add that brushing carries natural oil down the shaft; this has not been tested in published studies.
Risks and caveats: Hairbrush references list no specific hazards. Designs such as cushion and detangler brushes are intended to reduce breakage [1].
deepLead:
Boar bristle brushing means using a brush with natural boar hair bristles to smooth and style hair. Such brushes are described as having tightly spaced bristles that increase tension while brushing in order to smooth the hair .
Hair-care communities often say brushing spreads scalp oil along the hair and adds shine. Reference sources on hairbrushes do not make claims about oil distribution, and no clinical studies of this effect were found .

name: Haircut for face shape

angle.text: Styling and looksmaxxing advocates pick haircuts by face shape such as oval, round or square, to balance proportions. It is a popular rule of thumb with no published tests.

summary: Picking a cut by face proportions: a popular styling rule of thumb with no published tests behind it.
note: No studies of face-shape matching were found.
currentQuick:
This is the habit of choosing a haircut based on whether your face is oval, round, square and so on.
It is widely used by stylists, but no published studies testing the rules were found.
How it works: Practitioners say hair length and volume can make a face appear more balanced. Reference sources note that face shape is one of several factors in how a style looks [1].
Risks and caveats: The practice carries no reported medical risks; the main caveat is that its rules are untested.
deepLead:
Choosing a haircut for face shape is the practice of selecting a style to suit the proportions of the face, such as oval, round or square. Advocates in styling and looksmaxxing circles say particular cuts can balance or flatter particular facial proportions.
A general hairstyle reference notes that a style's look may depend on factors including face and head shape, hair type and growth patterns . No published studies testing face-shape matching rules were found, and encyclopedia coverage of facial shape treats it as anatomy and biology rather than a styling system .

name: Middle part / curtains / textured crop trends

chain: Frames face with fringe or texture
angle.text: Middle parts, curtains and textured crops are discussed as current men's cuts, with curtains linked to K-pop artists. The new look is visible once cut; no studies test effects on attractiveness.

summary: Middle parts, curtains and textured crops: trending cuts with a long history and no studies on their effect on attractiveness.
currentQuick:
Curtains are a long fringe parted in the middle, with shorter sides. Together with textured crops they are among the trending men's cuts discussed online.
History sources trace the look to early 20th century Britain and revivals since the 1980s; no studies test its effect on attractiveness.
How it works: Fans say the fringe frames the face and covers the forehead or sides of the head. This is a styling claim, not a studied mechanism.
Risks and caveats: No health risks are reported for the cuts themselves.
deepLead:
Curtains is a hairstyle with a long fringe divided by a middle or side parting, usually with shorter sides and back . In recent years it has been associated with K-pop artists, and middle parts and textured crops are discussed as current men's cuts.
Looksmaxxing forum users debate whether curtains or other cuts flatter facial proportions. No clinical studies exist on these trends, and the sources available document curtains' history more than any appearance outcome .

name: Gray hair reversal supplements

angle.text: People take copper, B12 and similar supplements hoping to restore natural hair color. Reversal is reported only where a deficiency caused the greying.

summary: Copper, B12 and similar pills marketed for restoring hair color; reversal is reported only where a deficiency caused the greying.
note: No supplement is reported proven to slow or reverse age-related greying.
currentQuick:
Some people take copper, vitamin B12 or other supplements hoping to bring back natural hair color.
Reference sources say no supplement has been proven to slow or reverse normal greying, though greying tied to a deficiency may reverse once the deficiency resolves.
How it works: Grey hair reflects loss of pigment-producing stem cells in the follicle. Proponents argue that supplying missing nutrients supports pigment production; this applies mainly to deficiency cases [1].
Risks and caveats: The sources used here do not list supplement-specific harms; deficiency testing and medical conditions such as thyroid disease are discussed in clinical literature as separate causes [1].
deepLead:
Gray hair reversal supplements are products and nutrients, such as copper and vitamin B12, that some people take hoping to restore natural hair color. Gray hair has no gray pigment; it results from reduced melanin production at the root .
Greying is attributed largely to genetics, and melanocyte stem cell loss is thought to trigger it . The Wikipedia article on greying states that no special diet, supplement, vitamin or protein has been proven to slow, stop or affect the process, while noting that greying linked to a deficiency such as B12 may reverse when the cause is resolved .
